title: 31 CFR 501.601 Records and recordkeeping requirements
pinpoint: 31 CFR 501.601 (full text); source note '89 FR 74834, Sept. 13, 2024'
summary: Every person engaging in a transaction subject to OFAC rules must keep full records for at least 10 years after the transaction date; holders of blocked property must keep records while blocked and for at least 10 years after unblocking.

title: 31 CFR 501.603 Reports of blocked, unblocked, or transferred blocked property
pinpoint: 501.603(a)(1)-(2); (b)(1)(i) initial report within 10 business days; (b)(2)(i) annual report of property held as of June 30 due by September 30
summary: Any US person holding blocked property must report it to OFAC within 10 business days of blocking and file an annual report each September 30 covering property held at June 30; primary duty rests with the holder; agents may file on its behalf.

title: 31 CFR 501.604 Reports of rejected transactions
pinpoint: 501.604(a)(1) who must report; (a)(3) 'transaction' definition; (c) within 10 business days; (d) via ORS
summary: A US person that rejects a transaction which is not blocked but would violate OFAC rules must report it to OFAC through ORS within 10 business days of the rejection.

title: Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations, final rule (90 FR 13286, FR Doc 2025-04864)
pinpoint: 90 FR 13286 Summary, Dates, Background paras 1-2
summary: Adopts without change the Sept 13, 2024 interim final rule (89 FR 74832) extending 501.601, App. A IV.B and 515.572 recordkeeping from 5 to 10 years; IFR effective date was March 12, 2025; rationale is Pub. L. 118-50 div. D s.3111 (10-year IEEPA/TWEA limitations period).

title: eCFR version history for 31 CFR 501.601 and 501.603
pinpoint: 501.601 substantive versions 2016-12-23, 2024-09-13, 2025-03-12; 501.603 latest substantive version 2026-07-27
summary: Shows the 10-year text took effect 2025-03-12; the 2026-07-27 change to 501.603 corresponds to OFAC's July 27, 2026 rule updating website/contact information (not a change to deadlines).

title: A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments
pinpoint: p.1 (five essential components; risk-based SCP; General Factors E/F); p.3 Risk Assessment (customers, supply chain, intermediaries, counter-parties); p.5 Internal Controls II and IV (IT calibration, recordkeeping); p.10 root cause VI (screening software faults), VII (due diligence)
summary: OFAC strongly encourages a risk-based sanctions compliance program with five components; risk assessment covers customers, intermediaries and counterparties; screening tools must be calibrated, updated for list changes and tested; OFAC considers program existence in penalty mitigation.

title: OFAC FAQs updated 2026-10-26 (FAQs 32, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, 53)
pinpoint: FAQ 36 (reject vs block; 'rejected transactions must not be processed forward'); FAQ 49 (ORS within 10 business days of the action); FAQ 53 (customer inquiry: 'there is nothing to reject', no reject report); FAQ 42 (blocking duty arises on receiving instructions and taking possession of funds)
summary: Blocking applies where a blocked person has an interest in property; rejection applies where a transaction is prohibited but nothing is blockable; a mere inquiry that is declined creates no reject report; reports go through ORS within 10 business days.

title: OFAC FAQ 5: How do I determine whether I have a valid match?
pinpoint: FAQ 5 steps 1-6 (date updated September 9, 2026)
summary: Six-step potential-match process: identify list, confirm OFAC nexus, compare identifiers (many alerts are false positives), follow internal procedures and check licenses, decide block/reject/proceed, document the investigation and report within 10 business days; OFAC does not confirm potential matches or false positives.

title: OFAC FAQ topic 1501 (Basic information) incl. FAQs 9 and 11
pinpoint: FAQ 9 (blocking = freezing; report within 10 business days); FAQ 11 (all U.S. persons must comply)
summary: Blocking freezes property without transferring title; blocked property is reported within 10 business days; all U.S. persons must comply with OFAC sanctions; FAQs do not mandate specific screening software.

title: OFAC FAQs added 2022-12-20 (FAQs 1105-1108) on humanitarian general licenses
pinpoint: FAQ 1105 (four GL categories incl. NGO activities; 87 FR 78470, 87 FR 78484); FAQ 1106 (FI reliance absent reason to know); FAQ 1108 (existing NGO GLs e.g. Iran not amended)
summary: December 2022 actions issued/amended GLs across many programs authorizing transactions incident to certain NGO humanitarian and other activities; existing program-specific NGO GLs remain; conditions differ by program.

title: 31 CFR 594.520 Authorizing certain transactions in support of NGOs' activities (Global Terrorism Sanctions Regulations)
summary: Authorizes transactions ordinarily incident to listed non-commercial civilian-benefit NGO activities (humanitarian, democracy, education, development, environment, peacebuilding) if the NGO is not blocked; excludes funds transfers with knowledge or reason to know the beneficiary is blocked (except taxes, fees, permits, utilities).

title: eCFR search: 'Authorizing certain transactions in support of nongovernmental organizations' activities' sections in Title 31
summary: NGO general licenses are codified program by program with different section numbers and possibly different conditions, so reliance must be versioned per program section and eCFR date.

title: 26 CFR 1.6001-1(e) Retention of records
summary: Records must be retained so long as their contents may become material in the administration of any internal revenue law.

title: Publication 4221-PC, Compliance Guide for 501(c)(3) Public Charities (Rev. 3-2018)
pinpoint: p.18 'How Long Should Records be Kept?' and 'Record Retention Periods'
summary: Keep records until the statute of limitations for the return runs (generally 3 years after due/filed date, whichever later); keep exemption application, determination letter, organizing documents and board minutes permanently; employment tax records at least 4 years; longer for non-tax needs.

title: Nacha Operating Rules, Subsection 2.3.2.7 (retention of consumer debit authorizations) as reported by secondary sources
pinpoint: Rule 2.3.2.7 cited by secondary sources; the fetched Nacha article (Nov 3, 2025) did not state the retention period
summary: Secondary sources consistently report originators must retain consumer debit authorizations for two years from termination or revocation and provide copies to the RDFI on request; not verified against the rulebook text.

title: 16 CFR 316.2(m) 'sender' (multiple marketers) and 316.3 'primary purpose'
summary: Where several persons' products are advertised in one email, each is a sender unless one is within the statutory sender definition, is identified in the From line as sole sender, and complies with listed duties. Primary purpose tests decide whether mixed messages are commercial; transactional/relationship content is defined in 316.3(c).

title: Definitions and Implementation Under the CAN-SPAM Act; Final Rule and Statement of Basis and Purpose (73 FR 29654)
pinpoint: 73 FR 29655, Part II.A.1 and n.17
summary: FTC rejected a blanket nonprofit exemption: CAN-SPAM 'does not set up a dichotomy between commercial and nonprofit messages'; nonprofit emails whose primary purpose is promoting a commercial product or service are covered; FTC lacks jurisdiction over non-profit entities but states and ISPs can sue them.

title: CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business
pinpoint: 'Monitor what others are doing on your behalf'; multiple-advertiser passage; opt-out 10 business days; penalty up to $53,088 per email (Jan 2024 figure)
summary: Both the company whose product is promoted and the company that actually sends may be held responsible; with multiple marketers all may be liable as senders; opt-outs honored within 10 business days and mechanism live 30 days.

title: 47 CFR 64.1200 Delivery restrictions (current text)
summary: Nonprofit calls ('by or on behalf of a tax-exempt nonprofit organization') need only prior express consent for advertising robocalls to wireless numbers; residential prerecorded nonprofit calls exempt up to 3 per 30 days with opt-out; revocation by any reasonable means honored within 10 business days; PEWC definition no longer contains one-to-one language.

title: 47 U.S.C. 227 (TCPA)
summary: Statutory 'telephone solicitation' excludes a call or message 'by a tax exempt nonprofit organization' (statute says 'by', the rule says 'by or on behalf of'); ATDS or prerecorded calls to wireless numbers need prior express consent regardless of caller status (no nonprofit exception in 227(b)(1)(A)).

title: Enhancing the Ability of Consumers To Control the Robocalls, Report and Order FCC 26-67 (91 FR 67214)
pinpoint: Dates (effective Nov 25, 2026); Discussion I.A; amended 64.1200(a)(10)-(12)
summary: Callers may treat revocation of an informational robocall/text as limited to that informational category; revocation of advertising/telemarketing revokes all such calls; callers may designate exclusive revocation means (IVR/key press, standard reply words, designated website/number); honor within 10 business days.

title: Modernizing the Ability of Consumers To Control Robocalls, FNPRM (FR Doc 2026-21820)
pinpoint: Abstract (FR API)
summary: Seeks comment on shortening the time to honor revocations, two-way texting requirements, a mandatory revoke-all method and treatment of affiliates. Not effective law.

title: Delete, Delete, Delete; Targeting and Eliminating Unlawful Text Messages (90 FR 42137)
pinpoint: Abstract (FR API)
summary: FCC conformed its rules to the court decision nullifying the first paragraph of the 2023 revised PEWC (one-to-one) rule; the court's mandate issued April 30, 2025, vacating the rule change as of that date.

title: Insurance Marketing Coalition Ltd. v. FCC, No. 24-10277, 127 F.4th 303 (11th Cir. Jan. 24, 2025)
pinpoint: Holding as summarized in search results; opinion not fetched
summary: Vacated the FCC's 2023 one-to-one consent and 'logically and topically related' requirements as exceeding TCPA authority (applying Loper Bright).

title: Campbell-Ewald Co. v. Gomez, 577 U.S. 153 (2016)
issuer: US Supreme Court (located via Wikipedia search result)
pinpoint: 577 U.S. at 156 (as reported by secondary sources)
summary: States, as undisputed, that a text message to a cellular telephone qualifies as a 'call' under 227(b)(1)(A)(iii). Not fetched; cited from search results and memory.

title: Steidinger v. Blackstone Medical Services, No. 25-2398 (7th Cir. July 14, 2026), as reported by Holland & Knight
issuer: Holland & Knight (secondary report of 7th Cir. decision)
pinpoint: Article summary
summary: Seventh Circuit held marketing texts are not 'telephone calls' under 227(c)(5) (private do-not-call claims), relying on McLaughlin Chiropractic v. McKesson (2025) limiting deference to FCC interpretations; 227(b) autodialed/prerecorded text claims unaffected.

title: 15 U.S.C. 78dd-2 (FCPA prohibited practices by domestic concerns)
summary: 'Domestic concern' includes any corporation, association or unincorporated organization with its principal place of business in the US or organized under US state law; no exception for nonprofit or charitable entities.

title: DOJ FCPA Opinion Procedure Release No. 10-02 (July 16, 2010)
pinpoint: pp.2-5 (three-stage due diligence; staged disbursement; independent monitoring and audit for 5 years; certifications); p.5 Analysis
summary: DOJ treated a US-organized nonprofit grantmaker as a 'domestic concern' under 78dd-2(h)(1)(B) and declined enforcement for a foreign grant given multi-stage due diligence, staged payments, independent monitoring/audit and grantee anti-corruption certifications. Binding only on the requestor.

title: DOJ Guidelines for Investigations and Enforcement of the FCPA (June 9, 2025), reported via secondary sources
pinpoint: Search-result summaries only
summary: DOJ ended the Feb 2025 (EO 14209) enforcement pause and reprioritized FCPA enforcement; the statute itself is unchanged. Not fetched.

title: NIST SP 800-63A-4 Digital Identity Guidelines: Identity Proofing and Enrollment
pinpoint: Sec. 1 IAL definitions; Sec. 2.5 KBV SHALL NOT be used for identity verification; Sec. 4.2 IAL2 approved non-biometric verification methods (confirmation code to validated address; proofing-agent visual comparison); fraud management/DIAS
summary: Final July 2025, supersedes 800-63A (2020). IAL1/IAL2 may be remote; IAL2 allows non-biometric verification options; IAL3 needs a proofing agent and biometric; KBV is not allowed for verification.

title: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management
pinpoint: Sec. 2.1-2.3 AAL definitions; 2.2.2 'Verifiers SHALL offer at least one phishing-resistant authentication option at AAL2'; 2.3.2 AAL3 non-exportable key, phishing resistance, syncable authenticators SHALL NOT be used at AAL3; 3.1.6.1 exportable keys usable at AAL2 or below
summary: AAL1 basic, AAL2 high, AAL3 very high confidence; AAL2 verifiers must offer a phishing-resistant option and may accept syncable authenticators; AAL3 requires a hardware-protected non-exportable phishing-resistant key.

title: NIST SP 800-63-4 Digital Identity Guidelines (CSRC publication pages for -4, A-4, B-4)
pinpoint: Date Published July 2025; supersedes SP 800-63-3 / 800-63B (03/02/2020); planning note 10/06/2026 implementation hub
summary: Confirms the -4 revision is final (published July 2025) and supersedes the 2017/2020 revision 3 documents.

title: Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc., 39 Cal.4th 95 (2006)
issuer: Supreme Court of California (via SCOCAL, Stanford)
pinpoint: Slip op. text: 'A business that adequately advises all parties to a telephone call, at the outset of the conversation, of its intent to record the call would not violate the provision'; fn. 10; choice-of-law discussion
summary: California's 632 applies to recording of calls with California residents by out-of-state businesses; advising all parties at the outset defeats a 632 claim because a party who does not wish to be recorded may decline to continue.

title: Smith v. LoanMe, Inc., 11 Cal.5th 183 (2021)
issuer: Supreme Court of California (via secondary summaries)
pinpoint: Holding as summarized; opinion not fetched
summary: Penal Code 632.7 bars parties as well as non-parties from intentionally recording covered cellular/cordless communications without consent of all parties.

title: 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d) (federal one-party consent)
summary: Not unlawful for a private person to intercept a communication where that person is a party or one party has consented, unless for a criminal or tortious purpose.

title: Reporter's Recording Guide - Introduction
issuer: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press
pinpoint: Introduction (all-party state list; interstate calls)
summary: Lists all-party consent states as California, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan (qualified), Montana, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and Washington; advises assuming the stricter state law applies to interstate calls; other RCFP pages note Connecticut and Nevada phone-call nuances.

title: Public Law 118-50, div. D, s.3111 (21st Century Peace through Strength Act) - IEEPA/TWEA limitations period 5 to 10 years
pinpoint: Described at 90 FR 13286 Background; statute text not fetched
summary: Extended the statute of limitations for civil and criminal IEEPA and TWEA violations from five to ten years.
